A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RLCracker and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial revision and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original watermark-removal experiments, baseline comparisons, and sensitivity and generalization studies in Section 5 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds adaptive-attack comparisons, robustness tests, transfer studies, and text-quality and distribution analyses.

M1.justification: The core GRPO and dual-KL attack remain. Appendix C.3 introduces an adaptation for Qwen3-8B using Qwen3-0.6B for KL rewards instead of the default attacker copy, and revises the written semantic-reward scaling from sigmoid(x) to 2 sigmoid(x)-1. These changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The original four corpora remain, while v2 adds C4 natural-text/continuation comparisons and evaluations against SemStamp, k-SemStamp, and the setting labelled RLWatermark/GAUSSMark. Unseen-key, cross-watermark, and mixed-watermark scenarios substantially expand the evaluated conditions beyond v1.

E2.justification: Appendix D.13 adds evaluated DPO attacks with 100 and 7,000 preference pairs, released DPO checkpoints, and watermark stealing (WS), including direct comparisons in Tables 16–19. WS was only discussed in v1. Think+SysP already appeared in v1's appendix, so its appearance in v2's main table is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: Mixed-key training changes from four keys, including the test key, to 100 distinct training keys with an unseen test key. New protocols include perplexity and GPT-4o judging, stronger KGW parameter settings, DPO training-budget controls, and mixed-watermark training with a separate validation set. These materially extend and revise the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's prompt, reasoning, training-size, weight-sensitivity, and generalization studies, v2 adds semantic-threshold sensitivity, certificate/removal correlation, proxy-model sensitivity, generator–attacker matching controls, cross-watermark transfer, mixed-watermark training, and human-distribution approximation analyses (Appendices D.8–D.16). These test important mechanisms and failure conditions previously unexamined.

E5.justification: Appendix D.9 and Table 12 newly report Pearson and Spearman correlation estimates between the certificate and removal rate. Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for attack-performance comparisons; the theoretical concentration bounds are separate from empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-8B RLCracker results, DPO/WS comparisons, quality scores, and robustness and transfer findings. Existing entries also change: Table 1's Qwen3-1.7B Think ESR on 1,500-token KGW selfhash changes from 76.3% to 66.3%. Mixed-key scores are replaced under changed conditions, while the headline 98.5% Unigram result remains.

T1.justification: Sections 3–4 redefine the distributional certificate around an input-conditioned local paraphrase distribution and formalize the semantic radius using output support and an infimum. v1's single-shot evasion proposition and Pass@k corollary are removed. v2 adds Proposition B.3, a bounded-variable proof of sub-Gaussianity allowing dependent tokens, and a dependence example.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion qualify the theoretical minimization claim as applying to a KL approximation and emphasize diagnostic stress-testing for watermark designers. The central detector-free RL attack, data-efficiency contribution, and headline empirical advantage remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes the KL certificate from the original semantic radius and explains its use by designers with detector statistics. New interpretations identify poor cross-watermark transfer and sensitivity to the watermark proxy, while discussing mixed-family training and harder semantic watermarks. These materially qualify v1's broad effectiveness narrative.

D1.justification: v2 announces code access through a repository link and adds the GPT-4o judging prompt, perplexity evaluator, Qwen3-8B reference-model exception and weights, and construction details for new experiments. Most existing Appendix C hyperparameters, software, hardware, and training-time disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands discussion of token-replacement, smoothing, DPO, and random-walk attacks. Section 4.1 also positions the distributional radius against Diaa et al.'s earlier robustness definition. This broadens the comparison with prior adaptive attacks beyond v1's mainly paraphrasing and proxy-model discussion.

P1.justification: The existing theoretical and methodological narrative is extensively rewritten with new explanatory headings and clearer distinctions between robustness notions. The title changes, Appendix A's LLM-use disclosure is replaced by extended related work, and the conclusion and impact discussion are reorganized. These exceed localized language editing.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, Table 1 is substantially expanded, and Figure 3's panels are rearranged side by side. New threshold-sensitivity and distribution figures, adaptive-comparison tables, and separate text-quality tables materially expand the visual presentation; numerous retained tables are relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through direct adaptive-attack comparisons, unseen-key evaluation, stronger watermark targets, and quality checks beyond P-SP. Its transfer and proxy studies expose meaningful limitations, while the revised theory clarifies the certificate's scope and supports its concentration assumption. These provide substantial gains over v1. Some overstatements and reporting inconsistencies remain, including D.13's blanket superiority wording versus Table 18 and unexplained low XSIR judge scores in Table 22.
